job.style: a diary entry or letter by a student

passage: Dear Diary, today in science class, we learned fascinating facts about our neighbourhood in space. Our teacher explained that the Sun is actually a star, not a planet, because it generates its own heat and light. It sits at the centre of our solar system, holding everything together with its massive gravity. We also discussed how the eight planets travel around the Sun. Interestingly, they do not move in perfect circles; instead, they follow elongated, oval-shaped paths called elliptical orbits. This means the distance between a planet and the Sun changes throughout its year. Later, we looked at the Moon through a telescope. It looked bright, but my teacher reminded us that the Moon does not produce its own light. It only shines because it reflects the sunlight hitting its surface, acting like a giant mirror in the night sky. It is amazing to think about how these celestial bodies interact. Earth is truly special because it has the perfect conditions to support life, unlike the other rocky or gaseous worlds nearby. I feel so lucky to live on this unique blue planet, floating through the vast, mysterious space. It makes me want to learn even more about the universe and our place within it.

items.evidence: Our teacher explained that the Sun is actually a star, not a planet, because it generates its own heat and light.
items.q: Why is the Sun called a star and not a planet?
options: It makes its own heat and light
It is much bigger and rounder than planets
It is the closest star to Earth
It sits still while planets move around
items.explain: The Sun is a star because it generates its own heat and light, as the teacher explained.

wrong.why: thinks being big and round decides what a planet is
mixes up closeness to Earth with the reason it is a star
thinks the Sun is still while everything circles it

items.evidence: Interestingly, they do not move in perfect circles; instead, they follow elongated, oval-shaped paths called elliptical orbits.
items.q: A planet's path around the Sun is drawn as a perfect circle. What is wrong with it?
options: Real orbits are stretched ovals, not circles
Real orbits are straight lines, not curves
Real orbits are circles around the Earth
Real orbits are circles of different sizes
items.explain: Planets follow elongated, oval-shaped elliptical orbits, so a perfect circle does not match their real paths.

wrong.why: still pictures the planets' paths as round circles
thinks the planets circle the Earth
thinks different sized circles fix the drawing

items.evidence: This means the distance between a planet and the Sun changes throughout its year.
items.q: A planet moves along an oval orbit. How does its distance from the Sun change?
options: It gets nearer and farther during its year
It stays the same during its year
It grows steadily larger every year
It changes only between day and night
items.explain: Because the orbit is an oval, the distance between planet and Sun changes throughout its year.

wrong.why: thinks circular paths keep the distance fixed
thinks the distance only keeps growing
links the Sun's effect to day and night

items.evidence: It only shines because it reflects the sunlight hitting its surface, acting like a giant mirror in the night sky.
items.q: Which everyday example is most like how the Moon shines at night?
options: A mirror flashing light from a torch
A lit candle glowing in a dark room
A bulb switched on by electricity
A glowing coal burning in a fire
items.explain: The Moon only reflects sunlight like a mirror; it does not make light as lamps and fires do.

wrong.why: thinks the Moon makes its own light like a flame
thinks the Moon is lit from inside like a bulb
thinks the Moon glows like a burning object

items.evidence: Later, we looked at the Moon through a telescope. It looked bright, but my teacher reminded us that the Moon does not produce its own light.
items.q: The Moon looks bright through a telescope. What does the teacher say about this brightness?
options: It comes from sunlight bouncing off the Moon
It comes from the Moon's own glowing rocks
It comes from the Earth's shadow on the Moon
It comes from the telescope making it brighter
items.explain: The Moon does not make light; it shines by reflecting sunlight that hits its surface.

wrong.why: thinks the Moon makes its own light
mixes Earth's shadow into the Moon's light
blames the telescope instead of the Sun
